subject: biology
title: Identifying the interaction between water molecules
stem: The schematic shows two water molecules. Which description of X is correct?

steps.text: Option A. Unequal electron sharing gives O a partial negative charge and H a partial positive charge; X is an intermolecular attraction between those sites.

options.label: D

subject: biology
title: A broken column in a leaf stalk
stem: A researcher introduces an air bubble into a water-filled xylem vessel while its leaf is transpiring. Water transport through this vessel decreases.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain how cohesion normally contributes to transport.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Suggest why the bubble disrupts this process.

steps.text: Hydrogen bonds create attraction between adjacent water molecules.
This cohesion allows tension generated at the leaf to be transmitted along a continuous water column.
The gas gap interrupts the continuous liquid column, reducing transmission of tension through it.

verification.notes: Scope checked against A1.1.1-6; contextual assumptions and mark points individually reviewed.

subject: biology
title: Climbing a narrow glass tube
stem: A clean narrow glass tube is placed vertically in water. Water rises above the level in the surrounding beaker.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Distinguish adhesion from cohesion in this observation.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why oil coating the glass could reduce the rise.

steps.text: Adhesion is attraction between water and the polar glass surface.
Cohesion is attraction among water molecules, which helps draw further water upward.
A non-polar coating reduces favourable interactions between water and the tube surface.

verification.method: Original syllabus-based authoring with explicit biological reasoning and recalculated data
verification.notes: Scope checked against A1.1.1-6; contextual assumptions and mark points individually reviewed.

subject: biology
title: Surface tension and a floating insect
stem: In a constructed demonstration, identical light wire frames are placed carefully on water. Eight of ten remain at the surface before detergent is added; one of ten remains after detergent is added.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the decrease in the percentage of frames remaining at the surface.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain a mechanism consistent with the observation.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: State one limitation of transferring this result directly to live insects.

steps.text: $80\%-10\%=70$ percentage points.
Detergent disrupts cohesive interactions at the water surface.
Reduced surface tension provides less support for the frames.
Insects differ from wire frames in features such as leg contact area or water-repellent surfaces; the model does not reproduce those features.

verification.method: Original syllabus-based authoring with explicit biological reasoning and recalculated data
verification.notes: Scope checked against A1.1.1-6; contextual assumptions and mark points individually reviewed.

subject: biology
title: Transporting solutes in blood
stem: A polar sugar dissolves readily in blood plasma, whereas a large non-polar lipid requires association with transport particles.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain the contrast in solubility.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why water is useful as a transport medium.

steps.text: Polar groups on the sugar form favourable interactions, including hydrogen bonds, with water.
The non-polar lipid cannot make equivalent favourable interactions with water and is poorly soluble.
Dissolved substances can move with the bulk fluid to tissues where they are used.

verification.method: Original syllabus-based authoring with explicit biological reasoning and recalculated data
verification.notes: Scope checked against A1.1.1-6; contextual assumptions and mark points individually reviewed.

subject: biology
title: Comparing heating of equal masses
stem: Equal masses of water and oil receive the same energy, with negligible energy loss. The water rises by $2.0\,^{\circ}\mathrm C$ and the oil by $4.0\,^{\circ}\mathrm C$. Which conclusion follows?

steps.text: Option A. For equal energy and mass, $c\propto1/\Delta T$; therefore $c_{water}/c_{oil}=4.0/2.0=2.0$. The greater capacity buffers temperature changes.

verification.method: Original syllabus-based authoring with explicit biological reasoning and recalculated data
verification.notes: Scope checked against A1.1.1-6; contextual assumptions and mark points individually reviewed.

options.label: A
options.text: Water has twice the specific heat capacity of the oil under these conditions.

options.label: B
options.text: Water has half the specific heat capacity of the oil.

options.label: C
options.text: Both liquids have the same specific heat capacity because their masses are equal.

options.label: D
options.text: The water received twice as much energy as the oil.

subject: biology
title: Temperature stability in a pond
stem:
A constructed comparison gives daytime and night-time temperatures of a pond and nearby air.

|Environment|Day / °C|Night / °C|
|---|---|---|
|Pond|19|16|
|Air|25|10|

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the temperature range in each environment.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain one property of water consistent with the smaller range.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why these data alone cannot establish that this property is the only cause.

steps.text: Pond: $3\,^{\circ}\mathrm C$; air: $15\,^{\circ}\mathrm C$.
Water has a high specific heat capacity, so a relatively large energy transfer is needed for a temperature change.
The environments also differ in factors such as mass, mixing, shading and heat exchange, which were not controlled.

verification.method: Original syllabus-based authoring with explicit biological reasoning and recalculated data
verification.notes: Scope checked against A1.1.1-6; contextual assumptions and mark points individually reviewed.

subject: biology
title: A seal in cold water
stem: A ringed seal and a land mammal have similar internal temperatures. Water conducts heat away from a warm surface more effectively than air.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain why this creates a challenge for the seal.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how a thick layer of blubber helps.

steps.text: A greater rate of heat transfer to the surroundings can cool its body more rapidly.
Blubber has low thermal conductivity and increases the distance over which heat must pass.
This reduces heat loss and the energy needed to maintain body temperature.

verification.method: Original syllabus-based authoring with explicit biological reasoning and recalculated data
verification.notes: Scope checked against A1.1.1-6; contextual assumptions and mark points individually reviewed.

subject: biology
title: Support and resistance in aquatic habitats
stem: Two aquatic animals are compared: a jellyfish with little rigid support tissue and a rapidly swimming fish with a streamlined shape.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Relate the jellyfish body plan to one physical property of water.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Relate streamlining to a different property.

steps.text: Water provides buoyant support, reducing the need for rigid structures to resist body weight.
Water is viscous and opposes movement through it.
A streamlined shape reduces drag for a given swimming speed.

verification.method: Original syllabus-based authoring with explicit biological reasoning and recalculated data
verification.notes: Scope checked against A1.1.1-6; contextual assumptions and mark points individually reviewed.

subject: biology
title: Why charged particles dissolve
stem: A student draws water around a positive sodium ion. Which orientation is most consistent with the polarity of water?

steps.text: Option B. The partially negative oxygen region is attracted to the positive ion. This solvation helps water act as a solvent.

verification.method: Original syllabus-based authoring with explicit biological reasoning and recalculated data
verification.notes: Scope checked against A1.1.1-6; contextual assumptions and mark points individually reviewed.

options.label: A
options.text: The oxygen and hydrogen ends carry equal positive partial charges.

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: D

subject: biology
title: Testing the effect of a leaf coating
stem: A student proposes that a wax-like non-polar coating lowers the adhesion of water to a leaf model. They compare the spread area of equal-volume droplets on coated and uncoated glass slides.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the independent variable and a measurement of the dependent variable.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: State two controls that improve the comparison.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why several droplets should be tested on each treatment.

steps.text: Independent variable: presence or absence of the coating; dependent variable: droplet spread area.
Keep droplet volume constant.
Use the same glass surface, temperature and time after adding the droplet; credit any one of these in addition to constant volume.
Replicates reveal variability and reduce the influence of an unusual droplet on the estimated treatment effect.

verification.method: Original syllabus-based authoring with explicit biological reasoning and recalculated data
verification.notes: Scope checked against A1.1.1-6; contextual assumptions and mark points individually reviewed.

subject: biology
title: Aqueous reaction compartments
stem: A freshwater unicellular organism contains many dissolved metabolites in its cytoplasm. During severe dehydration, movement of those metabolites and enzyme activity decline.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain two roles of water illustrated by the scenario.

steps.text: Water dissolves many substrates and products, allowing them to be distributed in the cytoplasm.
A fluid medium permits molecular movement and collisions required for metabolic reactions.

verification.method: Original syllabus-based authoring with explicit biological reasoning and recalculated data
verification.notes: Scope checked against A1.1.1-6; contextual assumptions and mark points individually reviewed.

subject: biology
title: Water delivery to a young planet
stem: A constructed model estimates that impacts delivered $8.0\times10^{18}\,\mathrm{kg}$ of asteroid material. The material was $12\%$ water by mass, and $25\%$ of the delivered water was retained.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the mass of water retained.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why this calculation does not prove that asteroids supplied all water on that planet.

steps.text: $2.4\times10^{17}\,\mathrm{kg}$.
The result depends on assumed impact mass, water fraction and retention; it neither measures every source nor excludes other sources.

verification.method: Original syllabus-based authoring with explicit biological reasoning and recalculated data
verification.notes: Scope checked against A1.1.7-8; contextual assumptions and mark points individually reviewed.

subject: biology
title: Retaining water after an impact
stem: Two hypothetical rocky planets receive similar water deliveries. One has much weaker gravity and a persistently hotter surface.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain two reasons why this planet may retain less water.

steps.text: Weaker gravity makes escape of water or its components to space easier.
High temperature keeps more water as vapour and may prevent its long-term condensation into surface reservoirs.

verification.method: Original syllabus-based authoring with explicit biological reasoning and recalculated data
verification.notes: Scope checked against A1.1.7-8; contextual assumptions and mark points individually reviewed.

subject: biology
title: Interpreting a habitable orbital zone
stem: An exoplanet lies within a star’s estimated habitable zone. Which conclusion is justified?

steps.text: Option C. The zone concerns conditions compatible with liquid water, not proof of water, an Earth-like atmosphere or life.

verification.method: Original syllabus-based authoring with explicit biological reasoning and recalculated data
verification.notes: Scope checked against A1.1.7-8; contextual assumptions and mark points individually reviewed.

options.label: A
options.text: Its atmosphere must contain exactly the same gases as Earth.

options.label: B
options.text: Its oceans must have the same salinity as Earth’s oceans.

options.label: C
options.text: Its orbital position may permit surface liquid water under suitable atmospheric conditions.

options.label: D
options.text: Living cells must already be present.

subject: biology
title: Selecting a follow-up observation
stem: Constructed observations describe planet P with a temperature compatible with liquid water but unknown atmosphere, and planet Q with spectral evidence of water vapour but a very hot surface.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Evaluate whether either observation alone establishes habitability.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Suggest one further measurement and explain its value.

steps.text: P’s temperature is compatible with liquid water, but atmospheric pressure/composition and water availability are unknown.
Water vapour at Q does not establish that stable surface liquid water exists.
Measure atmospheric pressure/composition or surface-temperature variation to constrain whether water could remain liquid; credit another relevant measurement with its link.

verification.method: Original syllabus-based authoring with explicit biological reasoning and recalculated data
verification.notes: Scope checked against A1.1.7-8; contextual assumptions and mark points individually reviewed.

subject: biology
title: Reading a nucleotide model
stem: A model labels a phosphate group P, a pentose sugar S and a nitrogenous base B. Which arrangement correctly represents one nucleotide?

steps.text: Option B. A nucleotide contains one sugar with an attached nitrogenous base and phosphate group.

verification.method: Original syllabus-based authoring with explicit biological reasoning and recalculated data

subject: biology
title: Two kinds of linkage in DNA
stem: A DNA sample is heated enough to separate its two strands while each strand remains a long polymer.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Distinguish the interactions disrupted from those retained.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why separated strands can pair again on cooling.

steps.text: Hydrogen bonds between complementary bases on opposite strands are disrupted.
Covalent linkages in each sugar-phosphate backbone remain intact.
Complementary bases can reform hydrogen bonds when suitable bases align.

verification.method: Original syllabus-based authoring with explicit biological reasoning and recalculated data
verification.notes: Scope checked against A1.2.1-10; contextual assumptions and mark points individually reviewed.

subject: biology
title: A complementary sequence
stem: One DNA strand contains the sequence A–G–T–C–C–A. Write the sequence on the complementary strand directly opposite it, reading in the same left-to-right direction on the page.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Deduce the complementary sequence.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why complementarity helps copying.

steps.text: T–C–A–G–G–T.
Each base on a template specifies which complementary nucleotide should pair with it, preserving sequence information.

verification.method: Original syllabus-based authoring with explicit biological reasoning and recalculated data
verification.notes: Scope checked against A1.2.1-10; contextual assumptions and mark points individually reviewed.

subject: biology
title: Recognizing RNA in a sample
stem: A nucleic acid contains ribose and uracil and is mainly single-stranded. Which identification is best supported?

steps.text: Option C. Ribose, uracil and a usually single-stranded chain are characteristic of RNA; DNA normally contains deoxyribose and thymine.

verification.method: Original syllabus-based authoring with explicit biological reasoning and recalculated data
verification.notes: Scope checked against A1.2.1-10; contextual assumptions and mark points individually reviewed.

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: A protein, because ribose is an amino acid.

options.label: C
options.text: RNA.

options.label: D
options.text: DNA, because all nucleic acids contain uracil.

subject: biology
title: Building a linear RNA strand
stem: A model assembles a single unbranched RNA chain of 25 nucleotides. Each new connection is represented as one condensation reaction.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine the number of connections between adjacent nucleotides.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: State what is removed in the simplified condensation model.

steps.text: There are $25-1=24$ connections.
One water molecule is removed per connection, giving 24 water molecules in this model.

verification.method: Original syllabus-based authoring with explicit biological reasoning and recalculated data
verification.notes: A simplified monomer condensation model is explicitly stated; this is not a claim about the full enzymatic nucleotide-triphosphate mechanism in cells.

subject: biology
title: Base composition in double-stranded DNA
stem: In a constructed double-stranded DNA sample, adenine forms $22\%$ of all bases.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage of thymine and of guanine.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why the same deduction need not work for a single-stranded RNA sample.

steps.text: Thymine is $22\%$ because A pairs with T.
Guanine is $(100-44)/2=28\%$ because the remaining bases are equal amounts of G and C.
A single RNA strand does not necessarily have a complementary partner imposing equal total A/U or G/C proportions.

verification.method: Original syllabus-based authoring with explicit biological reasoning and recalculated data
verification.notes: Arithmetic follows shared complementary pairing; it does not require historical Chargaff evidence, which is AHL.

subject: biology
title: Comparing two pentose sugars
stem: Ribose and deoxyribose each contain five carbon atoms. In deoxyribose, the group at carbon 2 differs from ribose.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State the difference at carbon 2.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Identify the nucleic acid normally associated with each sugar.

steps.text: Ribose has an OH group where deoxyribose has H.
RNA contains ribose, whereas DNA contains deoxyribose.

verification.method: Original syllabus-based authoring with explicit biological reasoning and recalculated data
verification.notes: Scope checked against A1.2.1-10; contextual assumptions and mark points individually reviewed.

subject: biology
title: Information in a short sequence
stem: A synthetic single DNA strand has eight positions, each of which can contain A, T, G or C. Assume no restrictions on sequence.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the number of distinct sequences.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why doubling the sequence length more than doubles the information-bearing possibilities.

steps.text: 65,536 sequences.
Each added position multiplies the number of possible sequences by four, so the number grows exponentially with length.

verification.method: Original syllabus-based authoring with explicit biological reasoning and recalculated data
verification.notes: Scope checked against A1.2.1-10; contextual assumptions and mark points individually reviewed.

subject: biology
title: A shared translation rule
stem: A researcher finds that the same mRNA codon specifies the same amino acid in two distantly related organisms. The result fits the broad conservation of the genetic code.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain how this supports common ancestry.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: State why one matching codon alone is limited evidence.

steps.text: A shared coding system can have been inherited from a common ancestor.
Conservation across distantly related groups is consistent with an ancient origin of that system.
A single match is a small sample; comparison across many codons and independent biological features gives stronger support.

verification.method: Original syllabus-based authoring with explicit biological reasoning and recalculated data
verification.notes: Scope checked against A1.2.1-10; contextual assumptions and mark points individually reviewed.

subject: biology
title: Correcting a DNA model
stem: A student’s model has A paired with C, G paired with T and a sugar-phosphate backbone made of weak hydrogen bonds.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Correct both base-pairing errors.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Correct the backbone description and state where hydrogen bonds belong.

steps.text: A pairs with T; G pairs with C.
The sugar-phosphate backbone contains covalent bonds.
Hydrogen bonds connect complementary bases across the two strands.

verification.method: Original syllabus-based authoring with explicit biological reasoning and recalculated data
verification.notes: Scope checked against A1.2.1-10; contextual assumptions and mark points individually reviewed.

subject: biology
title: Writing an antiparallel strand
stem: A DNA strand is written $5^{\prime}$–A–C–G–T–T–A–$3^{\prime}$. A researcher wants the complementary strand written from its own $5^{\prime}$ end to its own $3^{\prime}$ end.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine the required sequence, including end labels.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why reversing the left-to-right order is necessary.

steps.text: $5^{\prime}$–T–A–A–C–G–T–$3^{\prime}$.
The complementary strand runs antiparallel to the original, so its $5^{\prime}$ end is opposite the original $3^{\prime}$ end.

verification.method: Original syllabus-based authoring with explicit biological reasoning and recalculated data
verification.notes: Scope checked against A1.2.11-15; contextual assumptions and mark points individually reviewed.

subject: biology
title: Keeping a constant helix width
stem: A model DNA duplex has pairs of one two-ring base and one one-ring base. A proposed alternative pairs two two-ring bases together.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the two base categories.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why normal complementary pairs help keep the helix width constant.

steps.text: Two-ring bases are purines; one-ring bases are pyrimidines.
Each normal pair contains one purine and one pyrimidine and therefore has a similar overall width.
A purine–purine pair is wider and would distort the regular helix.

verification.method: Original syllabus-based authoring with explicit biological reasoning and recalculated data
verification.notes: Scope checked against A1.2.11-15; contextual assumptions and mark points individually reviewed.

subject: biology
title: Distinguishing nucleosome components
stem: In an idealized chromatin segment, 12 complete nucleosome core particles are present. Ignore any histone loss or exchange.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the number of core histone proteins.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why this is not necessarily the total number of histone molecules associated with the segment.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Describe the relationship of DNA to each core.

steps.text: Each core contains eight histones, so $12\times8=96$ core histones.
Additional linker histones can associate with linker DNA outside the eight-protein cores.
DNA is wrapped around the histone core rather than being replaced by protein.

verification.method: Original syllabus-based authoring with explicit biological reasoning and recalculated data
verification.notes: Scope checked against A1.2.11-15; contextual assumptions and mark points individually reviewed.

subject: biology
title: Tracing material entering bacteria
stem:
Constructed data from an experiment inspired by bacteriophage tracer studies are shown. Label P is attached to phage DNA; label S is attached to phage protein. After infection, blending and centrifugation, the bacteria form a pellet.

|Label|Recovered label in pellet / %|Recovered label in supernatant / %|
|---|---|---|
|P|82|18|
|S|12|88|

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify which phage component mainly entered the bacteria and cite the evidence.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how the result supports DNA as genetic material.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Give one reason the result is evidence rather than absolute proof.

steps.text: DNA mainly entered: 82% of its P label was in the bacterial pellet, compared with 12% of the protein S label.
The component entering cells is the candidate carrying instructions for production of new phages; DNA enters far more than protein.
Incomplete separation, residual attached phage or tracer contamination could account for some label in the unexpected fraction; further controls/replication are needed.

verification.method: Original syllabus-based authoring with explicit biological reasoning and recalculated data
verification.notes: Scope checked against A1.2.11-15; contextual assumptions and mark points individually reviewed.

subject: biology
title: Testing a repeating-base hypothesis
stem: A proposed model claims that every DNA molecule consists of equal proportions of A, T, G and C. Constructed analyses of two double-stranded samples give: sample X, A30%,T30%,G20%,C20%; sample Y, A18%,T18%,G32%,C32%.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Evaluate the proposed model using these results.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the distinction between rejecting this model and proving a replacement model.

steps.text: Both samples depart from 25% of each base, contradicting the equal-proportion prediction.
The samples still satisfy A=T and G=C, which is consistent with complementary pairing.
A failed necessary prediction can falsify the proposed model; agreement with some predictions supports a replacement but does not prove all its claims.

verification.method: Original syllabus-based authoring with explicit biological reasoning and recalculated data
verification.notes: Scope checked against A1.2.11-15; contextual assumptions and mark points individually reviewed.

subject: biology
title: Choosing a tracer control
stem: In a phage experiment, a researcher concludes that pellet radioactivity represents material inside bacterial cells. Which control most directly tests whether phages merely sticking outside the cells explain that signal?

steps.text: Option A. Removing external phage material while preserving intact bacteria separates surface association from entry into the cells.

verification.method: Original syllabus-based authoring with explicit biological reasoning and recalculated data
verification.notes: Scope checked against A1.2.11-15; contextual assumptions and mark points individually reviewed.

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.text: Use a longer exposure of the photographic film without changing the sample.

subject: biology
title: A compartment that is not yet a cell
stem: A laboratory vesicle encloses organic molecules and grows when additional lipid is supplied. It cannot copy information or maintain a network of energy-releasing reactions.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain why growth alone does not show that the vesicle is alive.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: State one useful role that this vesicle could nevertheless model in cell origins.

steps.text: Non-living assemblies can increase in size by adding material.
The vesicle lacks demonstrated self-replication of hereditary information and self-sustaining metabolism.
It models compartmentalization, which can keep internal chemistry distinct from the surroundings.

verification.method: Original syllabus-based authoring with explicit biological reasoning and recalculated data
verification.notes: Scope checked against A2.1.1-9; contextual assumptions and mark points individually reviewed.

subject: biology
title: Testing an abiotic synthesis model
stem:
A constructed experiment compares sealed gas mixtures exposed to electrical sparks. All mixtures initially contain no amino acids.

|Treatment|Spark|Amino acids detected after 5 days / arbitrary units|
|---|---|---|
|Mixture A|yes|38|
|Mixture A|no|2|
|Mixture B|yes|14|

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the difference between the sparked and unsparked samples of mixture A.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the conclusion supported by this comparison.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why the result does not establish the exact atmosphere of early Earth.

steps.text: The difference is $38-2=36$ arbitrary units.
Under the tested conditions, electrical energy is associated with a greater yield of amino acids.
The experiment tests selected gas compositions; it does not independently show which gases or concentrations actually existed on early Earth.

verification.method: Original syllabus-based authoring with explicit biological reasoning and recalculated data
verification.notes: Scope checked against A2.1.1-9; contextual assumptions and mark points individually reviewed.

subject: biology

stem:

|Specimen|Leaves|Leaf arrangement|
|---|---|---|
|P|simple|opposite|
|Q|simple|alternate|
|R|compound|opposite|
|S|compound|alternate|

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write a first pair of contrasting statements that divides the four specimens into two groups.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Complete the key so every specimen can be identified.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why an imprecise split such as “large leaves” versus “small leaves” may be less useful.

steps.text: 1a Leaves simple: go to step2; 1b leaves compound: go to step3.
Step2: opposite=P, alternate=Q.
Step3: opposite=R, alternate=S.
Without a measurable threshold the categories can overlap or depend on observer judgement.

subject: biology
title: Interpreting environmental DNA
stem: A constructed survey detects a fish DNA barcode in three water samples downstream of a lake but not in laboratory blanks.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain what conclusion is supported.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why this does not establish the number of living fish at each sampling point.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain the role of the blanks.

steps.text: DNA matching the fish is present in those samples, supporting its recent presence in the contributing environment.
DNA can persist or be transported, and shedding/detection rates vary; barcode detection is not a direct count of living fish.
Laboratory blanks test contamination from reagents or laboratory processing. Field blanks would be needed to assess contamination introduced during sampling.

subject: biology
title: Why classify organisms
stem: A researcher discovers an unfamiliar organism and assigns it to a well-supported evolutionary group.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain two practical benefits of doing so.

steps.text: Classification organizes and communicates information about biological diversity.
Shared ancestry allows testable predictions about features the organism may share with other members.

subject: biology
title: Ranks versus evolutionary history
stem: Two traditional families contain very different depths of evolutionary divergence. Which statement best explains why their equal rank is not an exact measure of relatedness?

steps.text: Option A. Rank is not a calibrated time scale; clade relationships are inferred from ancestry and evidence rather than equal labels alone.

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.text: All families must have exactly the same number of species.

subject: biology
title: Reading common ancestry
stem: Use the constructed cladogram.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the pair with the most recent common ancestor.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: State all terminal groups descended from node N1.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why W should not be described as the ancestor of the other present-day groups.

steps.text: Y and Z.
X, Y and Z.
W is a terminal group; the common ancestor is represented by an earlier internal node, not by a present-day tip.

subject: biology
title: Recognizing a complete clade
stem: In a rooted tree, a node has three descendant lineages P, Q and R. A proposed group contains P and Q but excludes R.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain why this group is not a complete clade rooted at that node.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain one advantage of using complete clades in classification.

steps.text: A clade contains the common ancestor and all its descendants, so R must also be included.
Membership consistently represents common ancestry rather than an arbitrary selection of descendants.

subject: biology
title: Comparing aligned sequences
stem:
A constructed alignment of the same homologous DNA region is shown.

|Taxon|Sequence|
|---|---|
|P|A C G T A A|
|Q|A C G T G A|
|R|T T G C G C|

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Count the differences between P and Q, and between P and R.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Suggest the closest pair on this evidence.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why more sequence data would strengthen the inference.

steps.text: P–Q: 1 difference; P–R: 5 differences.
P and Q have the greatest sequence similarity.
A short region may be unrepresentative or affected by chance similarity, selection or differing rates; independent regions provide a broader test.

subject: biology
title: A calibrated molecular clock
stem: For a constructed example, two lineages accumulate differences in a chosen region at a combined rate of 3 substitutions per million years. They differ by 18 substitutions. Assume the stated combined rate is constant.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Estimate the time since divergence.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why the result is an estimate rather than an exact date.

steps.text: 6 million years.
Mutation/substitution rates can vary with generation time, selection and other factors, so the constant-rate model is approximate.

verification.notes: Scope checked against A3.2.1-9; contextual assumptions and mark points individually reviewed.

subject: biology
title: Avoiding a two-lineage clock error
stem: A constructed molecular clock gives 2 substitutions per million years **per lineage** after divergence. Two sequences differ by 20 substitutions, with no reversals or repeated changes assumed.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the divergence time.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the error in dividing 20 by 2.

steps.text: Both lineages contribute, so $t=20/(2+2)=5$ million years.
It assigns all observed differences to one lineage and ignores changes accumulated on the other branch.

subject: biology
title: Choosing the most parsimonious model
stem: Two candidate cladograms explain a constructed character matrix. Tree U requires six changes and tree V requires nine changes under the same character model.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the tree preferred by parsimony and explain why.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why parsimony does not guarantee the true historical tree.

steps.text: Tree U is preferred because it accounts for the observations with fewer changes.
Real evolution can involve repeated changes, reversals or unequal rates; a simpler explanation may not match every historical event.

verification.notes: Scope checked against A3.2.1-9; contextual assumptions and mark points individually reviewed.

title: Rotating a branch at a node
stem: A cladogram is redrawn by exchanging the left-to-right positions of two sister groups without changing any connections. Which conclusion is correct?

steps.text: Option C. Relationships depend on branching connections and common ancestors, not the arbitrary spatial order of tips.

subject: biology
title: A morphology-based grouping is challenged
stem: Two constructed plant groups share a similar floral shape. Analysis of several independent DNA regions places each closer to a different group than to the other.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Suggest a biological explanation for the morphological similarity.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why the sequence evidence can support revising the classification.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: State one reason to inspect the molecular methods before revising the classification.

steps.text: Similar selection pressures may have produced convergent features independently.
Concordant evidence from several genes may better reveal ancestry than a single potentially analogous trait.
Errors in alignment, sampling, gene identification or tree inference could produce misleading relationships; credit a relevant concern.

subject: biology
title: Why compare ribosomal RNA
stem: A classification study compares homologous ribosomal RNA sequences from a wide range of organisms.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain one advantage of this evidence.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Name the three domains recognized by the resulting broad classification.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why the lack of a nucleus does not place all organisms in one of these domains.

steps.text: Ribosomal RNA occurs across cellular life and contains homologous sequences that can be compared across distant groups.
Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya (or Eukaryota).
Both bacteria and archaea lack nuclei but differ in molecular characteristics and ancestry.

subject: biology
title: Interpreting an internal node
stem: A diagram labels an internal branch point N. What does N normally represent in a cladogram?

steps.text: Option C. The node represents inferred common ancestry. Its exact date or phenotype requires additional evidence.

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.text: A measured extinction date even when no time scale is provided.

subject: biology
title: A clock affected by generation time
stem: Two constructed lineages diverged at the same time from a common ancestor. One has accumulated more substitutions in a neutral region. A candidate explanation is a higher number of generations per unit time.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain why this could affect a molecular-clock estimate.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why applying one rate indiscriminately could be misleading.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Suggest one improvement.

steps.text: More generations can create more copying opportunities per unit time, changing the apparent substitution rate.
A faster-evolving lineage may appear older if its extra differences are interpreted solely as extra elapsed time.
Calibrate rates with independent dated events and allow different rates for different lineages.

verification.method: Original syllabus-based authoring with explicit biological reasoning and recalculated data
verification.notes: Scope checked against A3.2.1-9; contextual assumptions and mark points individually reviewed.

subject: biology
title: Selecting homologous evidence
stem: A researcher compares a digestive enzyme in one species with an unrelated structural protein in another and uses the number of amino acid differences to estimate relatedness.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain the central problem.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Suggest a valid replacement comparison.

steps.text: The proteins are not established homologous versions of the same ancestral sequence, so aligned differences do not measure divergence from a shared sequence in the intended way.
Compare homologous genes or proteins across the taxa, using aligned corresponding positions and sufficient sequence length.

verification.method: Original syllabus-based authoring with explicit biological reasoning and recalculated data
verification.notes: Scope checked against A3.2.1-9; contextual assumptions and mark points individually reviewed.

subject: biology
title: Conflicting gene trees
stem: In a constructed study, one gene supports tree P and another supports tree Q. Each tree fits its own data strongly.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain why the conflict should not simply be hidden.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Suggest two ways to investigate it.

steps.text: Different genes can have different histories or methodological biases; the conflict is relevant uncertainty in the inference.
Compare additional independent genes or genome-wide data.
Check alignment, sampling and the possibility of gene transfer or other processes that make gene history differ from species history.

verification.notes: Scope checked against A3.2.1-9; contextual assumptions and mark points individually reviewed.

subject: biology
title: Using an evolutionary classification to predict a trait
stem: A newly sampled species is placed within a well-supported clade whose other sampled members all have a particular enzyme.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State a reasonable prediction.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why the prediction remains testable rather than certain.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Describe an observation that would challenge the prediction.

steps.text: The new species may also possess the enzyme or its homologous gene.
The lineage could have lost or modified the trait; direct genetic or biochemical evidence is needed.
Reliable evidence that the gene and enzyme activity are absent despite adequate detection controls would challenge it.

subject: biology
title: Recognizing an evolutionary change
stem: Which observation is sufficient evidence of an evolutionary change in a population?

steps.text: Option B. Evolution involves change in heritable characteristics of a population across generations; individual environmental responses or learning alone do not establish this.

options.text: Every individual becomes temporarily dehydrated during one afternoon.

subject: biology
title: Inherited change or environmental response
stem: A constructed study compares two plant populations grown in their native habitats. Population P has larger leaves. When offspring from both populations are grown under the same controlled conditions, their leaf-size distributions overlap almost completely.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain why the field difference alone does not demonstrate evolution.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how the offspring experiment changes the interpretation.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: State one limitation of concluding that the populations are genetically identical.

steps.text: Leaf size may differ because of environmental conditions rather than an inherited difference between populations.
A common environment removes some environmental differences; the overlap weakens the evidence that the field contrast is inherited.
One measured trait under one set of conditions does not test all genes or all possible inherited differences.

subject: biology
title: Comparing molecular evidence
stem: Constructed alignments compare the same 300-base DNA region in three mammal species. Species P and Q differ at 12 positions, P and R at 39, and Q and R at 36.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage sequence identity of P and Q.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Deduce which pair is most closely related according to these data.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why several independent regions would strengthen the inference.

steps.text: P and Q, because their aligned region has the fewest differences/highest identity.
A single gene may have an unusual evolutionary history or rate; agreement across independent regions provides stronger evidence of common ancestry.

subject: biology
title: Selection in a domesticated crop
stem: In a constructed breeding programme, only plants with the highest seed mass are used as parents. Mean seed mass rises from $2.4\,\mathrm g$ to $3.0\,\mathrm g$ over several generations in the same growing conditions.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage increase in mean seed mass.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why the procedure is artificial selection.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: State one reason the result does not mean every future seed must have a mass of 3.0 g.

steps.text: Humans choose parents according to a desired characteristic.
If variation in seed mass is heritable, selected parents pass relevant variants to offspring, changing the population across generations.
A mean allows individual variation, and both inherited differences and environmental effects can influence individual seed mass.

subject: biology
title: A shared limb pattern
stem: The schematic summarizes the same underlying forelimb arrangement in two mammals. P uses its forelimb mainly for swimming and Q mainly for grasping.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain why the limbs are homologous structures.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how their differences can arise while homology is retained.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: State one additional type of evidence that could test the proposed common ancestry.

steps.text: They share an underlying structural pattern inherited from a common ancestor, despite different functions.
Evolution can modify the size, shape or proportions of corresponding bones for different functions without removing their common origin.
Compare DNA/protein sequences, development or fossils; credit a relevant independent source.

title: Similar function with a different origin
stem: Insect wings are outgrowths of the exoskeleton; bird wings are modified vertebrate forelimbs. Both can provide powered flight. Which conclusion best describes this comparison?

steps.text: Option D. Similar selective pressures can produce convergent functional solutions from different ancestral structures.

options.text: The two flight surfaces must have evolved once in the most recent common ancestor of insects and birds.

subject: biology
title: Net change in a lineage’s species richness
stem: A constructed island lineage initially contains 8 species. Over a long interval, 5 speciation events each add one species and 3 species become extinct. Assume no immigration or emigration.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the final number of species.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why speciation and extinction must both be considered when interpreting diversity.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why the total alone cannot reveal which species survived throughout the interval.

steps.text: Speciation adds lineages while extinction removes them; their combined balance determines net change in species richness.
Different histories of origin and loss can produce the same final count; lineage-specific evidence is required.

subject: biology
title: A river and separated primate populations
stem: A hypothesis links divergence of the lineages leading to bonobos and chimpanzees to geographical separation associated with the Congo River.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain how a persistent river barrier can promote divergence.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why a barrier’s presence alone does not prove that it caused speciation.

steps.text: The barrier can reduce interbreeding/gene flow between populations.
Separated populations can accumulate different heritable changes under different selection pressures or by chance.
The timing of the barrier and lineage divergence must agree, and alternative causes or later contact must be considered.

verification.method: Original syllabus-based authoring with explicit biological reasoning and recalculated data

subject: biology
title: Testing a geographical barrier
stem: A constructed study compares fish in tributaries connected by open water with fish separated by a waterfall. Genetic differences are greater across the waterfall, but the separated sites also differ in temperature.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Suggest how the waterfall could contribute to genetic divergence.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why temperature is relevant to interpreting the result.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Propose one improvement to the study.

steps.text: It may restrict movement and interbreeding, reducing gene flow.
Different temperatures could favour different inherited variants, so divergence cannot be assigned solely to reduced movement.
Sample several matched connected and separated site pairs with similar temperatures, or measure movement and gene flow directly; credit a suitable design.

verification.notes: Scope checked against A4.1.1-7; contextual assumptions and mark points individually reviewed.

subject: biology
title: Independent evidence for common ancestry
stem: A constructed comparison groups species X and Y together using both their corresponding limb bones and several independent DNA regions. Species Z is more different by both measures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain why agreement between the two evidence types is useful.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why this conclusion does not require X to be the ancestor of Y.

steps.text: Independent anatomical and molecular observations support the same common-ancestry interpretation.

subject: biology
title: Speciation within the same region
stem: Two insect populations occupy the same geographical region but mate on different host plants and rarely exchange genes. Which description is most appropriate for a proposed speciation process under these conditions?

steps.text: Option C. Sympatric speciation occurs without geographical separation; ecological or behavioural differences can reduce interbreeding within one area.

subject: biology
title: Seasonal separation of flowering
stem: Constructed observations show that plant population P flowers mainly in weeks 1–3 and population Q in weeks 6–8. Their pollen can fertilize each other in hand-pollination trials and produce fertile offspring.

parts.label: a
